characterList.description: A young man with short, dark hair, glasses and a beard. He is wearing a dark-colored shirt and is sitting in front of a computer.
characterList.name: Brian Poww

content_metadata.description: A presentation by Brian Poww on the concept of scattering patterns in relation to Fourier transforms, focusing on various shapes and structures.

qAndA.answer: As the size of the sphere decreases, the period of the rings in the scattering pattern becomes larger.
qAndA.question: How does the size of a sphere affect its scattering pattern?

qAndA.answer: Babinet's principle states that the inverted image of an object will produce the same scattering pattern as the original object. This is demonstrated in the video with the sphere.
qAndA.question: What is Babinet's Principle?

qAndA.answer: When spheres of different sizes are present, their individual scattering patterns overlap due to the different frequencies of their oscillations, making it difficult to distinguish individual patterns.
qAndA.question: How does polydispersity affect the scattering pattern of spheres?

qAndA.answer: Regular structures like the lattice shown in the video produce diffraction spots in their scattering pattern.
qAndA.question: What type of scattering pattern do regular structures produce?

qAndA.answer: The presentation focuses on presenting factual information about scattering patterns and their relation to various shapes and structures. There is no underlying narrative or story being told.
qAndA.question: Does the presentation focus on telling a story or presenting information?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hello, I'm Brian Power and in this video I will be showing you some examples of scattering patterns.
For this purpose I have written a small program which you will be seeing in this talk.
As you may know what we see on the detector of a small angle scattering machine
is mathematically identical to observing the intensity of the Fourier transform of the real space electron density
It sounds complicated but it's just a way of saying that we take whatever sample we want to look at
put it through a mathematical operator and we end up with our scattering pattern.
This is fairly easy to do on a computer so this is what you are seeing here.
This display here shows you the output of my lapse of camera
on which I will show some examples of structures you will find in this samples.
On this display to my left over here you are right.
You see the intensity of the Fourier transform for the camera image.
In other words you can see what we will see on the detector of a small angle scattering machine for the sample.
Starting with a simple sphere you see that the detector shows us some repeating rings
for a smaller sphere.
The period of the rings becomes larger.
Due to the bobbin A's principle the inverted image gives us exactly the same scattering pattern.
Different shapes show different scattering patterns such as cubes,
squares which can be rotated and ellipsoids which can be also rotated.
You will see here that the oscillation frequency for the ellipsoid is highest in the long dimension
and lowest along the short dimension.
For dense but monodispir systems we still see these oscillations like this.
But when we introduce polydispiracy the oscillations of the spheres of different sizes,
different frequencies and overlap and therefore we cannot distinguish the individual oscillations anymore.
For the crystallographers among you regular structures such as this lattice will give you your diffraction spots.
So that's it. If you have a MacBook and a MATLAB download a copy of this program and start playing around.
Feel free to ask me if you have any question and let me know if you use this in any presentation.
Good luck. Bye bye.
Bye.

youtube_description:
A demonstration of a live Fourier Transform, which can be used to show the scattering (or diffraction) patterns from real-space projections. 
All recorded in a single take, I hope you do not mind the little errors here and there.
For more information and the software, go to http://lookingatnothing.com/
youtube_title: Live Fourier Transform demo, showing small-angle scattering patterns for some structures
